articles.title: Why Your 'Run Once' Trigger Guard Silently Skips Records
articles.excerpt: If your trigger handler uses a static boolean to "run once", it is probably skipping records in production, and nothing tells you. No error, no failed test, just records that never got processed. Sear…
articles.body: If your trigger handler uses a static boolean to "run once", it is probably skipping records in production, and nothing tells you. No error, no failed test, just records that never got processed. The pattern everyone copies Search for "Apex trigger recursion" and you'll find this in almost every tutorial: public class AccountTriggerHandler { private static Boolean hasRun = false ; public static void beforeInsert ( List < Account > accounts ) { if ( hasRun ) { return ; } hasRun = true ; for ( Account acc : accounts ) { acc . Description = 'Processed' ; } } } The idea is sound: if the trigger updates records and that update fires the trigger again, stop the loop. The static variable lives for the whole transaction, so the second run sees hasRun = true and exits.

articles.title: Stop your MQL5 EA from firing orders into a closed market
articles.excerpt: If your EA has ever filled its log with retcode 10018 (TRADE_RETCODE_MARKET_CLOSED), you know the pattern. A signal appears during the daily break, on a holiday, or a few seconds before the weekend cl…
articles.body: If your EA has ever filled its log with retcode 10018 (TRADE_RETCODE_MARKET_CLOSED), you know the pattern. A signal appears during the daily break, on a holiday, or a few seconds before the weekend close, and the EA tries again on every tick. Nothing is lost on that request, but retry logic, counters and alerts all get confused, and on a busy account it can look like the EA is broken. MT5 already knows the trading sessions for each symbol. You only have to ask. Reading the trade sessions SymbolInfoSessionTrade returns the start and end of each trading session for a given weekday. The times come back as seconds from midnight in server time.

articles.title: Test an avatar camera in Discord before an event
articles.excerpt: A private Discord voice channel is a convenient place to verify an avatar-camera setup before a community event. Join a test channel alone or with a colleague, open the camera preview, and confirm tha…
articles.body: A private Discord voice channel is a convenient place to verify an avatar-camera setup before a community event. Join a test channel alone or with a colleague, open the camera preview, and confirm that the intended virtual camera is selected. Check the microphone input separately; Discord can keep an old audio device even after the camera changes. Move through a few real speaking patterns: a normal greeting, a longer explanation, a pause, and a glance toward the chat window. Ask your test partner whether motion stays in sync and whether the image remains clear in the compact call layout. If the video becomes choppy, close other apps using the camera and try a lower output size before adjusting unrelated Discord settings.

articles.title: Choose avatar expressions that read well in webinars
articles.excerpt: Webinars often place the speaker in a small tile beside slides, so expressions need to stay readable without competing with the material. Before the event, list the moments when your face adds meaning…
articles.body: Webinars often place the speaker in a small tile beside slides, so expressions need to stay readable without competing with the material. Before the event, list the moments when your face adds meaning: welcoming attendees, emphasizing a key point, or reacting during questions. Use a restrained idle expression between those moments so viewers can focus on the presentation. Test the avatar at the actual tile size. Record a short opening, a sentence with emphasis, and a neutral pause. Review whether the expression changes are clear at a glance and whether they remain comfortable over several minutes. If a gesture or expression draws attention away from the slide, simplify it rather than adding more motion.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 15, 1988: The 300-foot Green Bank Telescope collapses suddenly, leaving a huge pile of wreckage in West Virginia
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 15, 1988, a 300-foot radio telescope in Green Bank, West Virginia suddenly collapsed. It happened at 9:46 p.m. on a clear night with no strong winds. When the observatory staff showed up to work the next morning, they were greeted by a huge pile of wreckage. The telescope collapsed under its own weight after a key structural element called a "gusset plate" failed. This was one of four connecting plates that held the telescope's large, metal beams together. Investigators found that these gusset plates were not built to last the 26 years that this telescope had been in use. Three years later, construction began on a new telescope. The Green Bank Telescope was even bigger and more sensitive, and it began science operations in 2001.

articles.body: For the past two years, stargazers have waited with bated breath for a "new" light to appear in the night sky, born of one of the most cataclysmic events known to occur in the cosmos — a nova explosion. But what is the "Blaze Star" T. Coronae Borealis, and why is it so difficult to predict when its overdue brightening will occur? We turned to the experts to find out. What is T. Coronae Borealis? T. Coronae Borealis — or T CrB for short — isn't a single star, but rather a binary system containing a dense white dwarf star and a bloated red giant. Over a period of around 80 years, the white dwarf's gravity strips material from the red giant until it hits a critical threshold.

articles.title: How escaping gases ripped apart a comet and caused it to become thousands of times brighter
articles.excerpt: This summer, comet 220P/McNaught burst into life out of nowhere to become one of the year’s highlights for amateur astronomers.
articles.body: A comet dazzled this summer as the sun’s heat caused ice beneath its surface to turn to gas and rip out through its surface, spewing hundreds of billions of pounds' worth of dust into space and causing the comet to brighten by thousands of times. Comet 220P/McNaught was discovered by the prolific Australian comet discoverer Robert McNaught in 2004. It is a periodic comet, the 220th discovered, meaning that it comes back again and again on a regular basis – in 220P’s case, once every five-and-a-half years when it gets about as close to the sun as Mars . Other than that, 220P is fairly nondescript, usually languishing at a feeble brightness fainter than magnitude +15, out of reach of most amateur telescopes. There has been little else to say about the comet, until this year.
